performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: The clarinet’s skipping refrain returns between episodes of long-breathed melody and quick runs. William McColl plays this A major rondo on his own handmade basset clarinet, whose low notes give the solo line an unusually deep reach.

sections.label: A · Clarinet skips above upper strings
sections.mNote: The A major refrain moves in lilting six-eight

sections.label: B · A longer tune for clarinet
sections.mNote: The solo line opens out towards E major

sections.label: A′ · A brief return to A
sections.mNote: The refrain returns before another orchestral departure

sections.label: Dev · The clarinet turns to F♯ minor
sections.mNote: Wide leaps and running figures above quiet strings

sections.label: B′ · The longer tune returns first
sections.mNote: Mozart brings back the episode before the full refrain

cues.title: A light-footed clarinet tune
cues.text: The clarinet begins a skipping tune in six-eight above violins and violas. Cellos, double basses and orchestral winds wait for the answering tutti. The upper strings leave plenty of space beneath the soloist’s first phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, opening, p. 242: solo clarinet and upper strings; cellos, basses and winds enter with the tutti.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coffee, tobacco and Stadler’s rondo
cues.text: Vienna, 7 October 1791: Mozart has coffee brought in and enjoys a pipe of tobacco. Writing to Constanze in Baden, he follows these domestic pleasures with a day’s work: “Then I orchestrated almost the whole of Stadler’s rondo.”
cues.evidence: Mozart to Constanze, 7–8 October 1791, Bauer–Deutsch 1193. Our translation of “dann Instrumentirte ich fast das ganze Rondó vom Stadtler”: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1193.pdf.

cues.title: The melody takes longer breaths
cues.text: The first episode gives the clarinet a more flowing melody and carries it towards E major. Short string replies support the longer solo phrases. The refrain’s little skips have opened into something more expansive.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first episode. Calvin Dotsey describes the complementary second theme: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A short visit from the refrain
cues.text: The A major refrain returns briefly. Its familiar rhythm is easy to recognise, but Mozart soon lets the orchestra carry the music away again. This homecoming is a short one.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first refrain return and ensuing tutti; Calvin Dotsey’s account identifies the brief return before the minor-key episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: F♯ minor beneath the runs
cues.text: The central episode turns to F♯ minor. The clarinet moves through wide leaps and running figures above quiet strings, with brief wind replies. Its bright upper notes and deep lower phrases now belong to a darker harmony.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, central solo episode, pp. 250–253. Calvin Dotsey discusses the minor-key central episode.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The second tune arrives first
cues.text: Mozart brings back the earlier episode’s melody before restoring the full refrain. The soloist has its longer-breathed tune again, while the skipping opening still waits. The familiar ideas return in an unexpected order.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, explicitly identifies the reprise of the second theme before the delayed principal refrain: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The skipping tune comes home
cues.text: The clarinet finally recovers the full refrain in A major. Upper strings accompany the return; the orchestral winds wait. The soloist still has room for further runs before everyone joins the closing phrases.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, final refrain, p. 257, and closing continuation.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A concerto survives without its autograph
cues.text: Mozart’s manuscript of the completed concerto is lost. Early printed editions adapt the solo for an ordinary clarinet, moving its lowest phrases upwards. Modern basset-clarinet versions recover the deeper compass for which Mozart writes.
cues.evidence: Calvin Dotsey, Houston Symphony, discusses the lost autograph, adaptations in the early editions and modern reconstructions: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/. Details of individual restored passages differ between editions.

cues.title: Everyone joins the last cadence
cues.text: Flutes, bassoons and horns join the strings for the closing tutti. The clarinet’s last trill gives way to the orchestra’s A major cadence. After so much nimble solo writing, the last chords are brisk and unanimous.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, closing page 264.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A longer solo turns towards E
transitions.from: A · Clarinet skips above upper strings
transitions.to: B · A longer tune for clarinet
transitions.how: The orchestral continuation of the A major refrain gives way to a longer clarinet melody over quieter strings. The solo phrases and changing bass lead towards E major. The six-eight pulse continues beneath the more sustained line.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first refrain and episode.

transitions.title: The clarinet restores A major
transitions.from: B · A longer tune for clarinet
transitions.to: A′ · A brief return to A
transitions.how: The first episode leads back through E, the dominant of A. The clarinet restores the skipping refrain in A major, with the strings supporting its familiar short phrases. An orchestral continuation soon moves the music on again.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, first return of the refrain.

transitions.title: The orchestra prepares F♯ minor
transitions.from: A′ · A brief return to A
transitions.to: Dev · The clarinet turns to F♯ minor
transitions.how: The orchestral continuation turns away from A major towards F♯ minor. Winds reinforce the cadence, then the clarinet resumes over quiet strings. Its wide leaps and running figures extend the new minor-key passage.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, orchestral lead-in and central solo episode, pp. 250–253.

transitions.title: The longer melody returns before the refrain
transitions.from: Dev · The clarinet turns to F♯ minor
transitions.to: B′ · The longer tune returns first
transitions.how: The central minor-key passage gives way to the earlier episode’s flowing clarinet melody. Quieter strings support the solo as it returns towards the home-key region. Mozart postpones the complete A major refrain, bringing the secondary tune back first.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III. The order of the returning themes is explained by Calvin Dotsey: https://houstonsymphony.org/swan-song-mozarts-clarinet-concerto/.

transitions.title: The clarinet steps back into A
transitions.from: B′ · The longer tune returns first
transitions.to: A″ · The skipping refrain comes home
transitions.how: The connecting passage brings the harmony back to A major. The clarinet begins the refrain over violins and violas, while winds and lower strings rest. The returning six-eight tune restores the light scoring of the opening.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1881), III, final refrain return, p. 257.

source.title: Mozart, Clarinet Concerto K. 622, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke XII/20 (1881), plate W.A.M. 622
source.locator: III. Rondo, printed pp. 242–264: refrain, episodes and final tutti. The solo instrument in this performance is McColl’s basset clarinet.

The clarinet’s minor-key phrases unfold above the strings.
The clarinet exchanges phrases with the strings as the longer melody returns.
The refrain returns above violins and violas, with winds and lower strings resting.
Orchestral phrases alternate with the clarinet’s continuing runs.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
